lines.text: Switchgear, dead, with the isolator handles all thrown the same way and a strip of tape across them somebody wrote on in 1994.
(again) Dead switchgear. Tape, and a date, and a hand that is not yours.
DEMOLITION NOTICE. Works commence 06:00 Thursday. The contractor is a name you have never heard of and the client is W. ELLERY HOLDINGS, which is the name on your work order.
(again) Six on Thursday. The board beside it still counts down in fourteens, and stopped being changed some time in March.
A piano lid, snapped across the hinge. Hymn books, swollen to twice their thickness. A lane rope from a pool that has been dry longer than you have been doing this.
(again) The building, in the order somebody decided it could be thrown away.
Forty stacking chairs under a tarpaulin, banded and labelled for collection. Somebody catalogued these. Nobody came.
(again) Still banded. Still labelled. Still here.
{range.use.replace(/^./,(c)=>c.toUpperCase())}. The {range.year} work is still legible under every later patch.
(again) The {range.year} range still gives the larger building its scale.
St Brendan’s Cathedral. Rubble stone, slate, a crossing tower and a west door with no exterior handle. Older than the conservatoire and outliving it.
(again) St Brendan’s Cathedral. Intact, disused, and shut from this side.
A short oak pew. The aisle end is dark with old hands; the rest has gone grey with dust.
(again) Dust in the mouldings. No service sheet.
The matching pew has a warped kneeler and a numbered brass plate.
(again) A number for a congregation that is not here.
Choir stalls under misericords blackened by age.
(again) The seat lifts. The carving underneath is worn smooth.
Choir stalls facing the empty centre line.
(again) No books. No cushions. No recent dust broken.
Louvre boards and their frame, down across the turret mouth. The stair behind them is full to the roof.
(again) Nobody is getting down this one.
Rubble from the turret vault, packed into the stair mouth to the ceiling.
(again) Not this way down.
An open stone pulpitum. Two flights of pierced tracery leave the centre passage clear.
(again) A screen that divides without sealing.
A battered octagonal font. The bowl is dry except for plaster grit.
(again) Stone dust in the bowl.
A brass lectern gone green at the joints. The service book is gone.
(again) The ribbon remains, marking air.
The altar stands one step above the choir. Linen and vessels were removed carefully.
(again) Bare stone and four pale footmarks.
A wall monument with its face and dates abraded before the cathedral closed.
(again) The name was removed deliberately.
A chest tomb pressed into the sacristy wall. Bird lime has found it even here.
(again) A stone sleeper under dust and feathers.
A visitor desk abandoned under dust. Its shallow drawers contain rubber bands, a pencil worn to the ferrule, and no money.
(again) The visitor desk keeps the shape of its last closing.
Guidebooks to St Brendan's, their tower diagram printed before the bell frame acquired this much dust.
(again) The same crossing, reduced to a clean black plan.
A dead donation till. The paper roll reads THANK YOU FOR HELPING US KEEP THE BELLS SOUNDING.
(again) No power. The last receipt remains uncut.
Postcards fade in a wire display: west front, crossing tower, eight bells, cold glass.
(again) Every card shows an entrance. None shows this way out.
A scarred dispatch desk, its pigeonholes still holding the previous shift. Somebody meant to come back to it.
(again) The open drawer is still waiting for the rest of its shift.
Your job is clipped over somebody else’s unfinished leaving.
(again) The last line is still waiting to be crossed out.
The route remains. The names beside it have been rubbed away.
(again) Three places and nobody assigned to walk between them.
A work lamp with its back open and its battery gone. An honestly dead thing.
(again) Click. Nothing. Good.
A hand truck tied up neatly before it ever carried the load.
(again) FRAME FIRST, still chalked across its foot.
Three empty crates. Everything in the room had somewhere to go except the chandelier.
(again) The empty boxes still smell of rain and hot dust.
A chandelier locked inside a wheeled cage. Its wire ends in open air.
(again) Too carefully held for rubbish. Too dead to be a lamp.
One chapel pew never made it upstairs. A paper removal tag is still tied to it.
(again) The tag says RETURN TO CHAPEL.
A percussion cart with one wheel wired straight.
(again) It will only travel in a circle.
Titian. Portrait of a Man. A Met Open Access reproduction in an inexpensive gilt frame.
(again) The sitter keeps looking past the entrance.
El Greco. Portrait of an Old Man. Someone has polished the glass more often than the frame.
(again) His eyes catch the corridor light first.
PUBLIC ENTRANCE. The glazed pair is chained under the closure order; the service entrance is around the block.
(again) PUBLIC ENTRANCE — CLOSED.
The ticket counter was built to keep a queue outside and cash inside. The grille is still locked down.
(again) Nothing has been sold here for years.
The staff desk is squared to the ticket window. A blotter has been pressed flat by damp.
(again) Front of house, stopped mid-week.
A staff chair tucked under the ticket desk, not abandoned in the queue path.
(again) Its casters have made a small grey ring.
A stack of folded programmes for a season that never opened.
(again) The top programme has curled at both corners.
A dead card terminal beside a cash drawer. The receipt paper is still threaded.
(again) No signal. No float.
A rekey ledger: REPLACEMENT LOCK — CHAPEL — CABINET C-17.
(again) CHAPEL. REPLACEMENT LOCK. C-17.
A key cabinet with the door off. Three rings left on a board cut for a dozen, each with a tag on it.
(again) The empty hooks are labelled too. Whoever kept this expected the keys back.
Tag: CH-04. CHAPEL — MAIN, stamped into the brass. The stamp is older than the ring.
(again) CH-04. The chapel door this was cut for is still there. The lock in it is not.
Tag: C-17. A cabinet number in biro, written over a scratched-out one.
(again) C-17. Newer than the ring it is on, and nobody has stamped it yet.
Tag: FOH-M. FRONT OF HOUSE — MASTER. Worn smooth on both faces.
(again) FOH-M. It opens everything on this side of the doors and nothing past them.
Programmes, float envelopes, and ticket stock boxed by week.
(again) The labels are more orderly than the room.
A notice board with staffing rotas, emergency contacts, and one hand-written refund policy.
(again) The refund policy is underlined twice.
A brass queue post with its rope still clipped in.
(again) The rope sags towards the ticket window.
A poster still in its frame: the last thing that was on. A Sunday, and nothing after it.
(again) Nobody took it down. There was no Monday to take it down on.
A price list under glass. Stalls, circle, restricted view, and a concessions line with three conditions on it.
(again) Restricted view is the cheapest seat and the only one that says what it is.
A bin by the doors, lined and never used. Someone put the bag in and that was the last of it.
(again) Clean, which out of everything in here is the strange part.
A roll of unsold tickets, still joined, still numbered. It stops in the middle of a Sunday.
(again) The tear is clean. Nobody hurried at the end of it.
The seating plan, drawn by hand and photocopied until the back rows went to grey.
(again) Two seats in the circle are inked out. No note as to why, and the ink is older than the copy.
A staffing rota for a fortnight that did not happen. Four names, one of them written in twice.
(again) The doubled name is down for both halves of the last night.
A till reconciliation, unsigned. It balances.
(again) Somebody counted it, agreed with it, and did not put their name to it.
A tray stencilled RETURNS, with nothing in it. The word came with the tray.
(again) RETURNED is the column the work order will not close without. Different building, same word.
A municipal waiting bench beside the ticket window. Its varnish is worn at regular shoulder-width intervals.
(again) People waited here facing the ticket window.
PUBLIC ROOMS: HALL, BATHS, CHAPEL, PRACTICE WING. Several arrows have been amended in three different hands.
(again) The building kept changing after the sign was made.
A glazed closure notice lists refunds, archive access, and a final public meeting that was cancelled.
(again) The cancellation is the newest paper in the case.
A wool rug under the waiting suite, and the reason it is still here is written across the middle of it in a stain nobody could lift.
(again) Ellery cleared this building to the walls. This stayed because it was worth less than the labour of rolling it.
Hessian drugget, tacked down the length of the room over the sprung maple. Somebody means to lift these boards before the machines come.
(again) Under it the floor is still a drum. Over it, walking is only walking.
A square of drugget upstage, rucked where something heavy was dragged across it and never straightened.
(again) The stage boards under it are unmarked. Everything either side of it is not.
A worsted runner fitted around the curved treads, with bound edges and a thin, compressed strip up the middle. The brass nosings remain exposed either side.
(again) The same central line of feet has thinned the wool. The edges kept their pile.
A corridor runner, rucked halfway along where a door has been dragged over it for years.
(again) It stops short of both ends. Whoever laid it measured once.
A runner up the centre of the nave, woven in quatrefoils to match the tracery it lies under.
(again) Everything else portable has gone from this room. Nobody has touched this.
A rug rolled and stood on end against the wall, tied twice and tagged at the top.
(again) The tag is a props number, not an inventory line. It came in for a production and never went out.
A pale foyer sofa from the formal front-of-house suite. FOH/F-01 is stamped beneath the centre rail; one cushion was rebuilt in a slightly firmer foam.
(again) FOH/F-01. The replacement cushion still sits higher than the others.
The first armchair of the foyer suite. FOH/F-02 remains on the rear rail, beside a hand-stitched repair where the public-facing arm wore through.
(again) FOH/F-02. The repaired arm has gone smooth again.
The matching armchair, FOH/F-03. Two dark blocks under the front feet are later than the chair and exactly the right height.
(again) FOH/F-03. A matched chair on unmatched blocks.
An armchair from the front-of-house suite, FOH/F-06, faced into the corner. The stamp matches the two still out in the atrium through this wall.
(again) FOH/F-06. It has been sat in since it was put here.

A tall-backed chair with dark green paint worn down to the wood. It belongs to no set: older than the suite and half a head higher, and somebody put it here facing the same way as the armchair, as though the two of them were waiting together.
(again) FOH/F-07. Two chairs, one conversation, nobody in either.
The last console of the suite, FOH/F-08, pushed against the atrium wall. The drawer is swollen shut and has been forced before — the lip is bright where somebody worked at it.
(again) FOH/F-08. Bright wood where the drawer was forced.

A large canvas, hung high on a picture rail that has no business being in a service corridor. It is the atrium's rail — the panelling comes through the wall here, half a metre of plaster between this room and the public one. The painting has been given the better half.
(again) Too big for the room and hung too high, on somebody else's rail.
A chandelier, in a corridor, over two chairs and a table. Nothing about this room was planned; all of it was moved here. Somebody went to the trouble of wiring it.
(again) It is still on the front-of-house circuit.
The west console of the foyer suite, FOH/F-04. A long pale tide mark follows the wall side; the inventory stamp is dry beneath it.
(again) FOH/F-04. Water above, old ink below.
The matching east console, FOH/F-05. Its top was refinished without touching the carved apron, leaving two different ages of varnish.
(again) FOH/F-05. The new varnish ends at the carving.
A small bronze horse study, accession ACC-41. The older paper label names no maker and records only that it arrived before the card catalogue.
(again) ACC-41. An object with a number and no useful beginning.
A marble bust, accession ACC-73. A clean steel pin through the old base says more about its history here than the blank sitter line.
(again) ACC-73. The sitter is still blank; the repair is fully documented.
CONCERT HALL — STALLS / GALLERIES. The gilt house lettering survives above the acoustic pair.
(again) CONCERT HALL.
A glazed programme case: winter concerts, municipal orchestras, school prize nights. The last season is crossed through in red pencil.
(again) The last season never opened.
Dry soil in a stone planter, packed hard and full of old leaf. Something black is coiled half down in it.
(again) The soil keeps the shape your hand left in it.
A flight case for the session microphones. The tape on its lid is marked with the room and the date they meant to come back. There is a pocket in the lid for blank stock.
(again) Packed properly. Not taken away.
A boom stand left at working height, its microphone still in the clip. The cable ends loose on the floor.
(again) Everything in place except the connection.
The numbered stage box and its heavy multicore, coiled for the control room. The free end is unplugged.
(again) They meant to wire it up again.
A Soundcraft Series 600, the sixteen-input version. Eight groups, a separate bank of tape monitors and a bridge of dark bar meters above the faders. The twin VU windows face the engineer.
(again) No pilot lights. No mains. The positions still mean something.
The rack is powered down. Three channels are still labelled in pencil.
(again) No mains. No pilot lights.
A closed metal spares tin on the shelf beneath the console, labelled for torch cells. One usable cell is inside.
(again) The spares tin under the console.
A session card on the console. One: voice. Two: room. Three has been carefully crossed out, but its fader is still set. In the margin, two chairs and fine lines to the glass.
(again) The third channel is crossed out. Its fader is still set.
A nearfield monitor with its cone pushed in and pulled back out.
(again) The cone remembers a thumb.
(again) It eats everything above four hundred hertz. Which is why the only thing left on the take is me.
A patchbay with every cable pulled, coiled and hung beside it. Somebody left this room tidy.
(again) You do not tidy a room you think is being knocked down. You tidy a room you are coming back to.
The engineer’s chair, facing the mixing desk and the room beyond the glass.
(again) Somebody worked in here for a long time, and then one day they did not come back.
A music stand, folded down and leant into the corner.
(again) Folded. You fold a stand you mean to come back for.
The mirrored wall, and the room in it is not quite the room. The sections are out of plane by a degree or so, so the far corner arrives twice.
(again) Two corners. One of them is the real one.
The long barre. Somebody has wound gaffer round a cracked bracket rather than replace it.
(again) The tape is older than the crack.
A stool at the height somebody left it.
(again) Still at their height.
A timetable in a wall frame, gone the colour of weak tea. Grades one to six, Tuesday and Thursday, and a note about outdoor shoes.
(again) Tuesday and Thursday, and nobody at all.
Chairs stacked four high in the short leg of the room, where they are out of the way of a class.
(again) Out of the way of a class.
A mirrored wall with a long diagonal crack across two sections, taped on the back so it holds together.
(again) Taped, and holding.
The barre here has been taken down at one end and left hanging, so it runs at an angle no dancer could use.
(again) Somebody started taking this room apart and stopped.
Rolls of sprung-floor vinyl stood on end in the corner, taller than you, taped at the top and furred with dust.
(again) Enough floor for a room nobody is going to lay it in.
A barre along the whole north wall, and the wall behind it is scuffed to shoulder height in one continuous band.
(again) The band is exactly where a hand steadies itself.
The mirror in here has been taken off the wall and stood facing it, so what is hung on the room is four feet of grey backing board.
(again) Somebody turned the mirror around. That is a decision, and it was made in here.
Chairs, stacked, in a room with the mirror facing the wall.
(again) Stacked, and waiting on a room that has been turned off.
A costume rail under dust sheets. Whatever is on it has kept its shape, which after this long means it was hung properly by somebody who cared.
(again) Hung properly, and left.
A dressmaker’s pin is caught in the chair lining. The seam beneath it is fresh.
(again) The pin is still caught in the lining. I am not putting a hand under there again.
B3, stencilled on the blockwork beside the opening. The work order in your pocket says the same thing.
(again) B3. The one they picked.
A Bronzino study, silverpoint and chalk. It looks unfinished because it is.
(again) The paper is paler than the wall.
Portrait of a Woman, Florentine, mid-sixteenth century. The brass plate gives no donor.
(again) No donor, only accession numbers.
The west hall chandelier, H/L-01, dark with the rest of the building. Its bottom chain links are newer than the matched fitting across the stalls.
(again) H/L-01. New chain, old fitting, no supply.
The matching east chandelier, H/L-02. Dust keeps the original suspension legible all the way to the ceiling rose.
(again) H/L-02. The pair was maintained separately and bought together.
A black Chesterfield at the rear cross aisle, H/S-01. Its machine-stamped plate is much later than the hand-marked foyer furniture.
(again) H/S-01. Newer stock, already worn at the aisle end.
The matching rear-aisle sofa, H/S-02. A square of unfaded leather marks where an information folder sat for years.
(again) H/S-02. The missing folder left its own label.
A stacking chair, set out and never stacked.
(again) Still facing the stage.
A music stand at sitting height.
(again) No part on it.
A metronome on the lid, still going.
(again) Still going.
A metronome on the lid, still going.
(again) Still going.
A metronome on the lid, still going.
(again) Still going.
A metronome on the lid, still going.
(again) Still going.
A metronome on the lid, still going.
(again) Still going.
A metronome on the lid, still going.
(again) Still going.
A green practice-room chair from the eight-chair order. {assetTag} is stamped underneath; {entry.state}.
(again) {assetTag}. One of eight, altered by this room.
A teaching desk waiting at the stair landing for somebody to claim it.
(again) Still waiting, safely out of the route.
The matching desk has been pushed alongside it, drawers to the wall.
(again) Two desks parked for collection.
A short pew, polished at the aisle end by hands.
(again) The aisle end is darker.
A matching pew, one kneeler missing.
(again) The empty brackets remain.
A painted sign over a gap in the east wall: TOWER — RINGING CHAMBER — NO ADMITTANCE TO THE PUBLIC.
(again) Somebody has added BELLS UP underneath it, in a different hand and a different decade.
The same sign at the chancel end, pointing back the way the stair comes down.
(again) The arrow was repainted at some point. It used to point the other way.
An electronics rack with the patch leads removed but every label left behind.
(again) The labels name feeds that are not here.
A plain altar table. The linen was removed; four pale rectangles show where its feet stood before it was shifted.
(again) Shifted, not deconsecrated.
A lectern with the service book removed and the ribbon left behind.
(again) The ribbon marks nothing.
The hymn board still reads 17 · 44 · 91. Nobody cleared the last service.
Piero del Pollaiuolo. Portrait of a Woman. Profile in tempera; gold remains along the edge.
(again) Her profile is exact and unreachable.
Portrait of a Woman, Netherlandish or French. The old label cannot decide.
(again) The frame can decide nothing either.
The first chapel lantern, EC/C-01, hangs dark. One pane is flatter and clearer than the rest, but the 1908 frame has never left its hook.
(again) EC/C-01. One new pane in an old, unpowered fitting.
The second lantern, EC/C-02. Its original rippled glass makes the torch break into narrow, unmoving lines.
(again) EC/C-02. Original glass, dead cable.
The third lantern, EC/C-03, was lowered by two chain links when the ceiling above the back pews was altered. The old links remain wired to the rose.
(again) EC/C-03. The alteration was retained instead of concealed.
The presider chair, EC/C-06: the one deliberate singleton in the 1908 chapel order. Wear reaches the finials but not the high centre panel.
(again) EC/C-06. Commissioned as one, recorded as one.
J. VALE & SONS — CAST FOR ELLERY COLLEGIATE CHAPEL — 1908. Eight bells. Tenor: 2,200 kg.
(again) Ellery Collegiate Chapel. 1908. No county is given.
The tenor sally hangs at the covering position. Seven bells are changing above it; this one is waiting for a hand.
(again) TENOR — 2,200 kg. Cover every row.
A full-circle rope, tied off above the sally. The bell above is down.
(again) Still tied. Still down.
A ringing bench polished by coats and waiting hands.
(again) Eight places. No ringers.
The second bench leaves the rope circle entirely clear.
(again) Nothing is stored inside the circle.
ELLERY COLLEGIATE CHAPEL — STEDMAN TRIPLES — 1908. A touch, not a peal.
(again) The gilt names have gone brown.
CLOCK HAMMER ISOLATOR. A red lever, mechanically linked.
(again) ISOLATE / SERVICE.
RINGING ROOM. The enamel letters are older than the electrical conduit.
(again) RINGING ROOM.
BELLS — AUTHORISED ACCESS. The final word has been underlined by hand.
(again) BELLS — AUTHORISED ACCESS.
The shutter winch is taking the whole frame through its pawl.
(again) Under load.
The west score cabinet, EC/C-04. Its replacement lock is square and recent against the 1908 ironwork; the key number is C-17.
(again) EC/C-04. New lock, old cabinet, C-17.
The matching east score cabinet, EC/C-05. Its original lock has seized shut; the old ironwork is worn bright around the keyhole.
(again) EC/C-05. Original lock, seized shut.
ORGAN LOFT / NAVE. An arrow follows the service stair down.
(again) ORGAN LOFT / NAVE.
NAVE / CHAPEL EXIT. The route continues through the narthex to the public doors.
(again) NAVE / CHAPEL EXIT.
Municipal baths rules under wired glass: shower first, no outdoor shoes beyond the blue line, children accompanied. Closing time has been pasted over three times.
(again) Shower first. Outdoor shoes stop at the blue line.
A green first-aid cabinet beside the entrance. The inventory card still lists eye wash, foil blankets and a resuscitation mask; the seal is broken.
(again) First aid. Seal broken, card still signed.
The pool clock stopped at twenty-seven past. Chlorine has greened the screws but not moved the hands.
(again) Still twenty-seven past.
A cork lifebuoy repainted until its name has disappeared. The rope is stiff with old pool water.
(again) Layers of municipal red. No readable name.
A slatted changing bench, grey from chlorine.
(again) The grain has lifted around every brass screw.
A second bench set below the cubicles, close enough for bare feet and folded towels.
(again) No towel ever dried here.
A pool-maintenance cart parked by the service corner, not beside the basin. A sealed battery sleeve is clipped under the handle.
(again) The warning labels have run; the empty sleeve remains under the handle.
The pool cart carries M/L-01, one of two portable inspection lamps. Its replacement lens clamp is bright, but the disconnected lead ends at the cart.
(again) M/L-01. A repaired lamp with nowhere to draw power.
A lifeguard chair on the east deck, facing across the pool.
(again) The rescue tube is gone.
A lane-line reel staged beside the starting end, one cracked float still wound onto it.
(again) The handle turns half a revolution.
A starting block, its number plate removed.
(again) Four bolt heads and a paler rectangle.
A basin drain furred white with old pool salts.
(again) The salts trace every slot.
The natatorium distribution panel, S/P-02, matches the plant-room and front-of-house boxes. Chlorine has lifted the paint beneath its lower lip; every breaker is open.
(again) S/P-02. Same installation, different air, no live circuit.
The front-of-house panel, S/P-03. Its typed circuit card lists the Scene Dock, foyer and box office; the main isolator is down.
(again) S/P-03. A neat card for three dead circuits.
The practice-floor panel, S/P-04. Room numbers have been pencilled over a typed teaching-wing schedule; every breaker is open.
(again) S/P-04. The pencil is newer than the dead ballast.
The academic-floor panel, S/P-05, is fixed to the loggia wall where the stair arrives. Gallery and classroom banks are listed separately; every breaker is open.
(again) S/P-05. Last in the numbered run, nearest the way down.
The plant-room distribution panel, S/P-01. It begins the same numbered installation as the later boxes upstairs; two typed labels have been corrected in pencil.
(again) S/P-01. The oldest corrections are still the clearest instructions.
A heating pipe running the length of the wall, and one isolation valve on it shivering under the load. Steam is getting out somewhere behind the wheel, in a thin continuous note.
(again) Still hissing. The gauge needle is hard against its stop.
HEADER 3 — ISOLATION. Back nut, then gland, then handwheel, in that order, all three home before the line is dead. Clockwise to close, and the card is emphatic about it.
(again) The last line is in a different hand: the bypass cock feeds the return and is NOT part of this header. Somebody learned that the hard way.
A Stillson nearly two metres long, left across the maintenance rack.
(again) Too large for the field case. It will have to travel on the floor.
The work lamp is still dead. It is the only light in the room that behaved.
(again) Click. Nothing. Somehow that is comforting now.
Black bulbs. Bright glass. Every wheel still locked.
(again) The cage never moved. The thing inside it changed anyway.
The case is not quite where you remember it. You never touched it, so memory gets the last word.
(again) A small distance. A large uncertainty.
The handle seems to have moved. You never marked it, so “seems” is all you own.
(again) One tooth past certainty.
The bar hums under your hand. You never knocked it before.
(again) The shutter is still. Something in it is not.
The case stayed here. Its little metal cough came from across the room.
(again) One sound. Two places. Keep them separate.
The handle did not turn. The click still came from behind the desk.
(again) You know what you heard. You do not know what heard you.
Your knock returned from above the chandelier, where there is no steel to carry it.
(again) The room knew the sound well enough to put it somewhere else.
Open scales and a marked examination piece cover the upright. The metronome stopped one click before the bar line.
(again) The examination piece is still open at the bad bar.
An upright turned slightly towards two offset chairs. The lesson stopped before anybody put the cello away.
(again) The piano is still angled towards the absent student.
The fallboard is off and the action has been interrupted halfway out. A service lead trails under the bench.
(again) The action remains halfway out.
A plain teaching piano with somebody’s coat and bag occupying the useful half of the room.
(again) The coat and bag make the room feel briefly claimed.
The upright has been pulled into a small rehearsal arc. Three parts disagree about where the first repeat begins.
(again) The rehearsal arc still points at the piano.
Copied parts have spread from the upright to the stand, chair, floor, and wastebasket.
(again) Every copy has a different pencil correction.
The upright is square to the wall. Everything else is skewed towards the door, as if the room left in a hurry.
(again) Only the piano kept its place.
